title: Paths, path connectedness, and convexity
terms: path; path-connected space; convex set; star-shaped set.

exposition.text:
A path from x to y is a continuous map p : [0, 1] → X with endpoints x, y. A space is path
connected if every pair of points can be joined by a path. Path connectedness implies connect-
edness because [0, 1] is connected; the converse fails.
In Euclidean space, a convex subset contains the segment (1 − t)x + ty between any two of its
points, and is therefore path connected. A punctured plane remains path connected because
a polygonal path can avoid the missing point, whereas removing a point from the real line
disconnects it. These provide useful dimensional distinctions.
A set is star-shaped if it has a point c such that the segment from c to every point of the set
lies in the set; unlike convexity, it need not contain segments between arbitrary pairs. Two seg-
ments through c give a path. A nonempty closed convex subset of finite-dimensional Euclidean
space has a unique nearest point to any given point: compact restriction gives existence, and
the strict midpoint distance inequality gives uniqueness.

question.text:
Which space is connected but not path connected?
(A) R \ {0}
(B) Q
(C) {(x, sin(1/x)) : 0 < x ≤ 1} ∪ ({0} × [−1, 1])
2
(D) R \ {(0, 0)}
2
(E) [0, 1]

solution.text:
The closed sine curve is connected because it is the closure of the connected graph over
(0, 1]. Suppose a path joined its vertical segment to the graph. In the parameter interval
where its first coordinate has just become positive, that coordinate is continuous and tends
to zero at the left endpoint. It therefore takes arbitrarily small values at which sin(1/x) = 1
and also values at which sin(1/x) = −1, arbitrarily near that endpoint. The second coordi-
nate could not be continuous there. Hence no such path exists. The punctured plane and
square are path connected, while the punctured line and rationals are disconnected.

Let A = {(x, y) ∈ R : xy > 0} and B = {(x, y) ∈ R : xy ≥ 0}. Which statement is correct?
(A) Both are connected.
(B) Neither is connected.
(C) A is connected and B is not.
(D) A is disconnected and B is path connected.
(E) A is path connected and B is disconnected.

solution.text:
A is the disjoint union of the first and third open quadrants, giving a separation. Every
point of B can be joined to the origin by a straight segment lying in B, and two such
segments join any pair of points.

question.text:

The set R \ {(0, 0)} is
(A) Convex
(B) Compact
(C) Connected but not path connected
(D) Path connected but not convex
(E) Disconnected

solution.text:
Two points can be joined by a polygonal path detouring around the missing origin. But the
segment between opposite points passes through the origin, so convexity fails.

question.text:
n
Every nonempty star-shaped subset of R is
(A) Open (B) Path connected (C) Bounded (D) Convex (E) Closed

solution.text:
Join each of two points to a star center by the segments contained in the set, then concate-
nate those segments. Star-shapedness is weaker than convexity, which requires every direct
segment.
